I wanted to used the fact that the conjugation map on complex number is an algebra-morphism over the reals. But, Lean does not have some kind of coercion in the background which recognises this, i.e. the following gave me an error

open ComplexConjugate

#check (conj : ℂ →ₐ[ℝ] ℂ)

So, when I needed the fact in my code, I created a have within my definition.

open ComplexConjugate
...
have : ℂ →ₐ[ℝ] ℂ := {
    toFun := conj
    map_one' := by simp
    map_mul' := by simp
    map_zero' := by simp
    map_add' := by simp
    commutes' := by simp
  }

This felt like a really silly have to have, because pretty much everything above is proven using simp. Is there is a better way to do this?

And in your tactic body, you probably meant let, since have is for proofs and throws away the body of the declaration. So if you have it, you wouldn't be able to differentiate your declared hom from something like id.
In Mathlib, we don't usually have coercion of bare functions into more bundled homs. They're usually packaged as separately named declarations.
@Yakov Pechersky thanks a lot. I did use have in my case, and it did not cause any problems. Could you elaborate a bit more on why I should have used let instead - I don't entirely understand
In your proof, imagine you wrote have f : ℂ ≃ₐ[ℝ] ℂ := { toFun := conj, ...}. How would you show have : f.toFun = conj := rfl? You won't be able to.

The declaration f is two things, a type of a term and the body of the term. have only retains the type, since that suffices for proofs (proofs for the same type/proposition are axiomatically equal). let, on the other hand, retains the body as well.
I tried to find an explanation about this in #tpil but couldn't locate one

@Yakov Pechersky thanks a lot. You do not need to go looking for another explanation - what you've typed above make total sense to me. Luckily in my case, I just needed the fact that it had the correct type - so I did not encounter any problems, but I definitely see why let is preferred over have in such scenarios.
Then for your proof, what happens if you use AlgHom.id R C instead?

I did not use it in a proof, but rather in a definition. So I could theoretically have used AlgHom.id R C as well. But, I needed conjugation. I am guessing the problem you mentioned would show up later, when I tried to actually make use of that definition.

I am guessing the problem you mentioned would show up late

It will not, have vs let is only an issue if you need the assignment immediately
Oh, okay. That's good to know. Thanks!
